                       Rock–paper–scissors and Lizards

  Playing games is an essential part of the human experience. Games are a safe
way of exploring real–life situations, allowing us to develop ways of predicting how,
given certain rules, events will unfold and to plan accordingly. They teach us about
chances and unpredictability, which play such essential parts in nature’s game of
life.
  From ancient civilizations all around the world, we have a fascinating selection of
games: stones thrown in the sand, sticks tossed in the air, coins placed in holes
carved into wooden blocks, hands used to compete, and pictures drawn on cards.
From ancient Mancala to Monopoly, from the game of go to the poker tables of
Vegas, games are invariably won by whoever  is best at taking a mathematical,
analytical approach.
  Jan–ken–pon  in  Japan,  ro–sham–bo  in  California,  kai–bai–bo  in  Korea,  and
ching–chong–cha  in South Africa — the game of rock–paper–scissors  is played  all
around the world. The rules are very simple: on a count of three, each player
makes his or her hand into one of three shapes: a fist for a rock, a flat hand for
paper, or two fingers in a V for scissors. Rock beats scissors, scissors beat paper,
and paper beats rock. Two of the same is a draw.
  Now, the reason for the first two wins is clear: rock breaks the scissors, scissors
cut the paper. But why does paper beat the rock? A sheet of paper isn’t much
protection against someone throwing a rock at you. But  it may be that  this
convention goes back to ancient China, in the days when a petition to the king
was symbolized by a rock. The king would indicate whether he’d accepted the
petition by placing a piece of paper above or below the rock.  If the rock was
covered by the paper, the petition was refused and the petitioner defeated.
  The origins of this game are hard to trace. There is evidence that it was played
in the Far East and by Celtic tribes, and even possibly as far back as the ancient

   Egyptians, who used to play finger games. However,  all these cultures seem to
  have been beaten to the discovery by a group of lizards that have been playing
  the game in the fight for survival long before human beings were making fists.
    The West Coast of the United States is home to a species of a lizard known as
  the common side–blotched  lizard. The male comes  in three  different  colors —
  orange, blue, and yellow — and each color has a different mating strategy. Orange
   lizards are the strongest and will attack and beat blue lizards. The blue lizards are
  bigger than the yellow lizards and are happy to engage in battle with them and
  beat them. But though the yellow lizards are smaller than the blue and orange
  males, they look like female lizards, and that confuses the orange lizards. So the
  orange lizards, who are looking for a fight, don’t notice the yellow lizards slipping
  under their gaze and mating with the females. The yellow lizards are sometimes
   referred to as “sneakers” for the sneaky way in which they beat the orange ones.
  So orange beats blue, blue beats yellow, and yellow beats orange — an evolutionary
   version of rock–paper–scissors.
    These lizards have been playing the game in the course of perpetuating their
  genes for a long time, and  it would be interesting to know whether they have
  developed a strategy for winning. Their population tends to follow a six-year cycle
   in which first orange dominates, then yellow, then blue, then orange once again.
  The pattern that emerges is precisely the one that people will use in trying to win
  the game in one–to–one combat. See too many rocks being thrown and you start
  to offer paper, but once your opponent sees the run of paper beating the stone,
  he or she wises up and switches to scissors to cut off your paper run. You soon
   pick up your opponent’s change of behavior and shift to rock.
    At its heart, winning this game is all about spotting patterns, and that’s a very
  mathematical  trait.  If you can predict what your opponent  is going to do next
  because of a pattern of behavior he or she has established, then you’re  in. The
  problem is that you don’t want there to be any immediately obvious rhythm in the
  way you respond, or your opponent will gain the upper hand. A huge amount of
  psychology  is going on as each contestant tries to spot patterns in his or her
  opponent’s play, each second–guessing what the other might do next.

                         What Is Culture?

     The word culture has many different meanings. For some  it refers to an
    appreciation of good literature, music, art, and food. For a biologist, it is likely
   to be a colony of bacteria or other microorganisms growing in a nutrient
   medium in a laboratory Petri dish. However, for anthropologists and other
   behavioral scientists, culture  is the  full range of learned human behavior
    patterns. The term was  first used  in  this way by the pioneer  English
   anthropologist Edward B. Tylor in his book, Primitive Culture, published in
   1871. Tylor said that culture is “that complex whole which includes knowledge,
    belief, art, law, morals, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired
   by man as a member of society.” Of course, it is not limited to men. Women
   possess and create it as well. Since Tylor’s time, the concept of culture has
   become the central focus of anthropology.

                                Is Culture Limited to Humans?

     There is a difference of opinion in the behavioral sciences about whether
   or not we are the only animal that creates and uses culture. The answer to
    this question depends on how narrowly culture is defined. If it is used broadly
   to refer to a complex of learned behavior patterns, then  it is clear that we
   are not alone in creating and using culture. Many other animal species teach
    their young what they themselves learned in order to survive. This is especially
   true of chimpanzees and other relatively intelligent apes and monkeys. Wild
   chimpanzee mothers typically teach their children about several hundred food
   and medicinal plants. Their children also have to learn about the dominance
   hierarchy and the social rules within their communities. As males become
   teenagers, they acquire hunting skills from adults. Females have to learn how
   to nurse and care for their babies. This kind of knowledge is not hardwired
    into their brains at birth. They are all learned patterns of behavior just as they
   are for humans.

                      Genome Editing

  The dream of  precisely and accurately changing almost any part of any
genome — even in complex species such as humans — has become a reality due
to recent progress  in genome  editing. But with great power comes great
responsibility, and the ease with which this process can now be performed has
brought the ethics of genome editing to the public's attention.
  Genome editing makes  it possible to change specific DNA sequences with a
great degree of control and precision, and there are abundant ways in which it
can be used, from developing new crops to improving human health. There are
a variety of techniques, but the most revolutionary involves using CRISPR, or
clustered regularly inter-spaced short palindromic repeats — parts of DNA that
work with enzymes to cut strands of DNA at specific locations.
  The use of CRISPR in genome editing has prompted calls for a genome editing
moratorium from a group of concerned US academics. Because it is the easiest
technique to set up and so could be quickly and widely adopted, the fear is that
it may be put into use far too soon — outstripping our understanding of  its
safety implications and preventing any opportunity to think about how such

  powerful tools should be controlled.
    While ethical concerns over genetic modification are not new, particularly when
    it comes to humans, they have intensified with the introduction of genome
   editing for a number of reasons. First, there is no clear consensus as to whether
  genome editing  is  just a further step forward, or whether  it represents a
   disruptive technology capable of overcoming the current orthodoxy. If this is the
  case — and  it is a very real prospect — then we will need to carefully consider
  genome editing’s ethical implications and whether current regulation is adequate.
    Second, there are significant ethical concerns over the potential scope and
   scale of genome editing. As more researchers use CRISPR to achieve more
  genome changes, the effects shift. Our consideration of a technology that is
   rarely used and then only in specific cases will differ from one that is widely used
   for  many   different  purposes,  because  without  oversight  and   careful
   consideration, there could be all kinds of unpredictable consequences.
   Genome editing techniques have so far been used to change genomes in
   individual cells and in entire nonhuman organisms. Benefits have included better
  targeted gene therapy  for some  diseases  in  animals.  Genetic  modification
  through genome editing of plants has already created crops that are resistant
  to herbicide and infection.
    But more controversial is how genome editing might be used to change traits
   in humans. While this has been the basis for many works of science fiction, in
   real life our capacity to provide such genetic engineering has been substantially
   limited.
   Genome editing potentially changes  this, presenting us with the very real
   possibility that any aspect of the human genome could be manipulated as we
   desire. This could mean eliminating harmful genetic conditions or enhancing
   traits considered advantageous. But  this  ability may also open the door to
  eugenics, where those with access to the technology could select for future
  generations based on traits considered merely desirable: eye, skin or hair color,
  or height.
     Currently, modifying plants, some animals, and non-inheritable cells in humans
   is allowed under  strict controls. But  in general, modifications that  alter the
  human germ-line are not allowed.

could be used for altering the human germ-line: that is, making gene alterations
inheritable by our children. Gene therapies that produce non-inheritable changes
in a person's genome are ethically accepted, in part because there is no risk for
the next generation  if things go wrong.
  Germ-line alterations pose much greater ethical concerns since a mistake could
harm future individuals. Of course, the flip-side is that, if carried out safely and
as  intended,  germ-line  alterations  could  also  provide  potentially permanent
solutions to genetic diseases.
  There is no doubt that genome editing has enormous potential to enhance and
extend human life, and these are benefits that we can all agree on. But what is
giving so many scientists unease is the potential that genome editing could be
used in unpredictable and ultimately disastrous ways. That is why so many argue
that we ought to tread lightly and err on the side of caution, especially when it
comes to altering the very fabric of what makes us human.

             Forensic Linguistics and the Case of Derek Bentley


  There are cases where linguistic clues have helped solve actual crimes. The story
of Derek Bentley is a powerful example. Bentley was not a typical teenager — he had
an IQ of just 77 and was unable to even write his own name. On November 2, 1952,
he and his 16-year-old friend, Christopher Craig, attempted to rob a warehouse in
Croydon, South London. A young girl saw them, and her mother alerted the police.
When the officers arrived, Craig shot and killed one of them. Although Craig pulled
the trigger, Bentley was arrested, charged, and ultimately convicted of murder. On
January 28, 1953, at the age of 19, Bentley was hanged.
  Bentley did not fire the gun, but he was accused of encouraging Craig by allegedly
shouting, “Let him have  it.” Both boys denied that Bentley had said anything to
provoke the shooting. However, the police submitted Bentley’s confession as evidence,
claiming  it was a verbatim record of his words, offered voluntarily and without
prompting. The jury reached a guilty verdict in less than two hours.
  Bentley’s family never accepted this outcome. For decades, they fought to clear his
name. Finally, in 1998, the case reached the Court of Appeal, where a forensic linguist,
Professor Malcolm Coulthard, played a crucial role. Coulthard analyzed the confession
and demonstrated that it could not have been Bentley’s spontaneous speech. Instead,
the language revealed signs of police influence — evidence that Bentley had been
guided or questioned during the confession process.
  One key clue was Bentley’s use of denials that didn’t fit the context of the narrative.
In natural  storytelling, people describe what did happen — not what  didn’t. For
example, someone is unlikely to say, “I didn’t see a dog,” unless asked, “Did you see
a dog?” In Bentley’s statement, he said, “Up to then Chris hadn’t said anything.”  Yet
at no point in the narrative had Bentley mentioned that Chris had spoken. This remark
suggested he was responding to questions — questions that were not recorded, but
likely asked during interrogation.
  Another revealing feature was Bentley’s use of the word then. In everyday speech,
most people use the word order “Then I...” rather than “I then...”. However, in Bentley’s

the police. Since the confession was a major part of the case against him, this
undermines its credibility and supports the view that Bentley’s conviction was unjust.

   It was a calm October afternoon, the kind that makes everything feel slow and quiet.

I sat in the drawing room, pretending to reread a book. The window was open, as usual.

The air was warm, but  I had something cooler in mind.

  Mr. Nuttel arrived, just as my aunt had expected. He looked uncomfortable even

before he said a word. His shoulders shook a bit, and he kept glancing around like

the room might collapse.  I smiled.

  "My aunt will be down presently," I said sweetly. "In the meantime, you must try and

put up with me."

  He nodded, stiffly, and  I could already tell he was the perfect subject.  I asked him

a few questions, enough to confirm he didn’t know a thing about us. That’s when  I

began.

    I told him the story of the tragedy: the swamp and the missing men. My voice

dropped slightly as  I spoke, and  I stared out the window, my fingers curling slowly

around the arm of the chair.

  "They never came back,"  I said, softer now. "Poor Aunt Sappleton keeps the window

open every evening..."

  He said nothing, but  I could feel his attention sharpen.  I added a few more details

— the waterproof coat, the song Ronnie used to sing.  I let my voice falter at just the

right moment.

  Then my aunt came in, cheerful and normal. Too normal. Mr. Nuttel looked pale.

  When the three of them actually appeared—guns under their arms, spaniel trotting

behind — I didn’t need to say a word. He bolted.

 A pause. Then  I said, “I expect it was the spaniel. He told me he was once chased

into a grave by wild dogs.”

  Romance at short notice? Oh yes. It’s always been my speciality. (289단어)

 평가한다. 이때 선정 이유의 타당성, 본문 근거의 명확성이 주요 평가 기준이 된다. 또한 보다 창의

 적인 글쓰기를 평가하고자 할 경우에는 원작에서 거의 드러나지 않은 그 외 등장인물(Framton’s

  sister, the husband, the two young brothers, and the dog)을 선정하고 원작의 흐름에 맞도

 록 상상하여 쓰도록 지도할 수 있다.

∙ Step 2에서는 작품 속에서 해당 인물의 말과 행동을 명확하게 근거로 찾아내었는지를 확인한다.

 확인한 근거를 바탕으로 인물 간의 상호작용 관계를 구체적으로 설명하고, 중심 인물과 주변 인물의

 상호작용을 정확하게 표현했는지를 평가한다.

∙ Step 3에서는 선정한 인물의 시점으로 서사를 구성하는 활동으로, 인물의 시점에 맞게 원작의

 감정·행동·상황을 적절한 언어 사용을 통해 서술하였는지를 평가한다.

∙ Step 4에서는 다른 모둠의 글을 읽고 비판적으로 감상하고 피드백을 제공하는지를 평가한다. 모둠

 에서 선택한 문장의 의미 파악, 관점 전환의 효과 이해, 원작과의 비교 감상 등 해석과 성찰이

 잘 드러났는지 확인하며, 이 과정에서 글쓰기 성찰 능력과 평가 참여 태도도 함께 확인한다.

∙ 채점 기준표의 채점 요소별 1점의 수행 특성보다 부족한 수행 특성을 보이는 경우는 0점으로 처리한다.

   A team of researchers from the University of Oviedo in Spain mapped the genetic

   To trigger rejuvenation, the researchers put the jellyfish under stress by letting
 them go hungry. As the medusae got smaller, changed into little balls called bud
  polyps, and began remaking their adult bodies, the scientists took pictures of what
 genes they were using in each phase of their development. They took some jellyfish
  in each phase, froze them, and crushed them into a thick mixture to extract their
 mRNA, creating a record of which genes were actively being used to make proteins.
   They also compared Turritopsisdohrnii to Turritopsisrubra, a related jellyfish species
 that ages normally. Researchers found that, compared to its relative, the “immortal
  jellyfish” has double the amount of genes that repair and protect DNA. This allows
 Turritopsis dohrnii to produce more restorative proteins.

 with reproduction and stem cell population. Normally, during the process of DNA
 copying and cell division, the protective end-caps on chromosomes, called telomeres,
  slowly get shorter and shorter, and when they are too short, a cell enters senescence

   Nurses’ Right
   Nurses face ethical dilemmas on a daily basis regardless of where they practice.
 There is no ‘right’ solution to an ethical dilemma. Ethics involve doing good and causing
 no harm. But how one defines what is ethical varies from nurse to nurse and depends
 on their individual values, beliefs and experiences.
   There are many ethical issues nurses can experience. Patients’ quantity versus quality
 in life is one of them. Quantity may address how long a person lives or perhaps how
 many people will be affected by the decision. Quality relates to how good a life a
 person may have, and the answer varies depending on how a person defines good.
 When a patient may live longer, but will likely experience significant side effects from
 the therapy, what should the nurse’s position be?
   Another issue is the dilemma between patients’ freedom and the control of the
 freedom. Does a patient have the right to make choices for one’s self that may result
 in harm, or should the nurse prevent this choice? For example, a patient wants to
 stop eating, but the nurse knows the consequences will harm the patient. In this
 situation, does the nurse have the ‘right’ to force the patient to eat despite the patient’s
 freedom to stop eating? Or do they have to value the patient’s choice because the
 decision is about his or her body after all?
  Whether nurses have to tell the truth or intentionally give incorrect information
 to patients and their families is a well-known ethical issue faced by medical staff.
 It becomes clear especially when families want to disagree over telling the patient
 the truth about the medical condition. What should a nurse do when a family insists
 that telling the patient the result will cause harm? How can a nurse know if this
 is true? Does the patient have the right to know?
   Ethical dilemmas in nursing come daily in which they must make a decision. A possible
 procedure to deal with them may be obtaining a second opinion from other nurses
 or doctors.

   논술형


Read the article “How Cold Is Absolute Zero?” and complete the following
two-step task. [18점]


   How Cold Is Absolute Zero?
    In principle, there is no upper limit to temperature. As thermal motion increases,
 a solid object first melts and then vaporizes. As the temperature is further increased,
 molecules dissociate into atoms, and atoms lose some or  all of their electrons,
 thereby forming a cloud of electrically charged particles—a plasma. Plasmas exist
  in stars, where the temperature is many millions of degrees Celsius. Temperature
 has no upper limit. In contrast, there is a definite limit at the opposite end of the
 temperature scale. Gases expand when heated, and they contract when cooled.
 Nineteenth century experimenters found that all gases, regardless of their initial
 pressures or volumes, change by 1/273 of their volume at 0℃ for each drop in
 temperature of 1 degree Celsius, provided that the pressure is held constant. So,
  if a gas at 0℃ were cooled down by 273℃, it would contract 273/273 volumes and
 be reduced to zero volume. Clearly, we cannot have a substance with zero volume.
   The same is true of pressure. The pressure of a gas of fixed volume decreases
 by 1/273 for each drop in temperature of 1 degree Celsius. If it were cooled to
 273℃ below zero, it would have no pressure at all. In practice, every gas converts
 to a liquid before becoming this cold. Nevertheless, these decreases by 1/273
 increments suggested the idea of the lowest temperature: -273℃. That’s the lower
  limit of temperature, absolute zero. At this temperature, molecules have lost all
  available kinetic energy. No more energy can be removed from a substance at
 absolute zero.  It can’t get any colder.
   The absolute temperature scale is called the Kelvin scale, named after the famous
  British mathematician and physicist William Thomson, First Baron Kelvin. Absolute
 zero is 0 K (short for “zero kelvin”); note that the word ‘degrees’ is not used with
  Kelvin temperatures. There are no negative numbers on the Kelvin scale.  Its
 temperature divisions are identical to the divisions on the Celsius scale. Thus, the
 melting point of ice is 273K, and the boiling point of water is 373K.

   It means that each main character has a decisive tragic flaw—Hazel’s is her severe

[Step 2]

 The Fault in Our Stars refers to the idea that some problems in life are beyond

human control. In the novel, Hazel and Augustus both suffer from cancer, which was

not caused by any fault of their own. This contrasts with Shakespeare’s original line,

which claims that we are responsible for our fate. Hazel and Augustus, however, see

their suffering as written in the stars—a matter of fate, not choice. Augustus tries to

make meaning out of his life despite his illness, while Hazel tries to protect those she

loves from the pain of her disease. The title reflects their belief that not all tragedies

are the result of personal flaws, but rather the result of uncontrollable circumstances.

[Step 1] Text Reading: What Are Microaggressions?

 What Are Microaggressions?

   The term “microaggression” originated from Harvard University professor Chester
 Middlebrook Pierce in his work with Black Americans. He defined microaggressions
 as  subtle,  stunning,  often  automatic,  and  nonverbal  exchanges  that  are
  “put-downs.” Microaggressions have the potential to impact any oppressed group
  psychologically and can be linked to racism, genderism, and other forms of
  oppression.
    Racial microaggressions, such as assumptions about a person’s intelligence or
 work ethic based on their race or ethnicity, are commonplace verbal, nonverbal, or
 environmental indignities, whether intentional or unintentional, that communicate
  hostile or negative racial insults. Similarly, unfair and unequal treatment of women
 can manifest in discriminatory hiring or hostile work environments. Moreover,
  experiential microaggressions are also common and can be seen in statements that
  dismiss an individual’s cultural background or experiences. These microaggressions
 make target groups feel unwelcome, isolated, and unsafe.
   A  specific instance  involving a man with  visual impairment  highlights how
 microaggressions affect individuals with disabilities. When people speak to him,
 they often raise their voices. A well-meaning nurse was actually “yelling at him”

Title: The Hidden Harm of Everyday Words: Understanding Microaggressions

  Have you ever said something you thought was harmless, only to find out it hurt

someone deeply? These subtle actions or comments are known as microaggressions.

They are small, often unintentional, but they send negative messages to marginalized

groups.

  For example, imagine a student from another country being told, “Wow, your English

is so good!” Although the speaker may intend to compliment, the hidden message is

that the student is an outsider who doesn’t belong.

  These everyday comments may seem insignificant, but they can lead to feelings of

isolation, stress, and low self-esteem. Over time, they create barriers and reinforce

inequality.

 We can  all make a difference. Think before you speak. Ask yourself: Could this

comment carry an unintended message? By becoming aware and changing small

behaviors, we can create a more respectful and inclusive world.


Lecture Style(Speech)

  Hello everyone, my name  is [Student Name], and today   I want to  talk about

something we often overlook—microaggressions.

   First, let me ask you this: Have you ever been asked, “Where are you really from?”

At first, it might sound like an innocent question. But to the person being asked, it

may suggest: “You don’t belong here.” Microaggressions are subtle words or actions

that send  hurtful messages to people from marginalized groups. They may be

unintentional, but they have real consequences. They can make someone feel invisible,

unworthy, or unwelcome.

  Let me share a quick example. A visually impaired man was often shouted at by

people trying to help him. They thought they were being kind, but their raised voices

implied he was less capable in all aspects. Imagine how that must have felt.

  So, what can we do? We need to listen, reflect, and choose our words carefully. Most

importantly, we must  learn  from  the  perspectives  of  those who  experience

microaggressions. Small changes in our language can lead to big changes in someone’s

life. Thank you.

 Many students identify consciously or unconsciously as nomophobes when  it
 comes to using cell phones. ‘Nomophobia’ is the fear of being away from a

  phobia.’ A feeling of anxiety washes over people suffering from nomophobia
 when they lose contact with their phones. Signs of nomophobia are easy to
  notice. Never turning  off the phone, taking the phones everywhere, and
  obsessively checking missed texts and calls are clear signs. Using phones at
  inappropriate times and missing opportunities for face-to-face interaction and
  preferring over the phone contact are indicators as well. Physical side effects
 can occur for nomophobes when their phone dies or is otherwise unusable.
 These symptoms include panic attacks, shortness of breath, sweating, increased
  heart rate, or chest pain. Millions of people suffer from nomophobia around the
  globe. The most common sufferers are in the 18–21 age range, making high

    thoughtful  consideration.  It may be  said  that  listening  involves more  active
     participation from a person than simply hearing. During communication, taking the

  Have you ever tried food that’s spicy, sour, and full of tradition all at the same time?

radish, and chili pepper. One of the best places to experience it is the Kimchi Museum

in Seoul, where you can learn its history and even make your own kimchi! Kimchi is

more than just a side dish—it’s a symbol of Korean culture. While it can be compared

to sauerkraut in Germany or pickles in the U.S., kimchi has a unique taste and is deeply

kimchi-making season. To enjoy it fully, try making kimchi yourself in a hands-on class.

and cultures, kimchi is a delicious place to start.

   An ethical dilemma is a situation where  it is difficult to say what is right or
  wrong. The Trolley Problem is a well-known example. A trolley is running out of
  control, and if it stays on its current track, it will hit five people. You have the
  option to flip a switch and send the trolley onto another track, where only one
  person is tied. In this case, doing nothing means five people will die, while taking
  action  will cause one person’s death. This situation creates a  difficult moral
  question: Should we act to save more lives, or avoid being responsible for killing
  someone? Some people follow Utilitarianism, which says the best action is the one
  that benefits the most people. From this view, flipping the switch is the right
  choice. Others believe it is wrong to take an action that directly causes someone’s
  death, even  if more people are saved. These different opinions show that even
  simple decisions can involve complex moral values.

      Ecotourism means  all  nature-based forms  of  tourism  in which  the main
    motivation of the tourists is the observation and appreciation of nature as well as
    the traditional cultures prevailing in natural areas. They are experiences that are
   managed to ensure they are ecologically, economically and socially sustainable,
    contributing to the well-being of the natural areas and local communities where
    they  operate.   It  contains  educational  features  for  those  interested   in
    understanding and preserving the nature and  local  culture. To minimize the
   damage massive commercial tourism may cause,  it  is exclusively organized by
    specialized tour operators for small groups. Service provider partners at the
    destinations  tend  to  be  small,  locally owned  businesses.  Consequently,   it
    generates  economic  benefits  for  the  host  communities,  organizations  and
    authorities managing natural areas with conservation purposes, promoting the
    awareness towards the conservation of natural and cultural assets, both among

  Jeju Gotjawal Forest is a unique and beautiful place located on Jeju Island, South

Korea. What makes it special is that it sits on ancient lava rocks, creating a unique

ecosystem. The forest is filled with green trees, mossy stones, and quiet trails. Even

in summer, it stays cool and peaceful, making it a perfect place to escape the heat

and enjoy nature.

  You can get to Gotjawal Forest by taking a bus or taxi from Jeju Airport. It takes

about 40 minutes. Visitors can walk along eco-trails, breathe in clean, fresh air, and

listen to the sounds of birds. Local people run eco-programs through which tourists

can learn about native plants, plant trees, or help clean the forest. There are also local

products like Jeju honey and herbal tea sold by the community to support the local

economy.

    I recommend Gotjawal because it is rewarding and relaxing. It is not crowded like

other tourist spots, so people can enjoy its peace and quiet. The forest shows how

tourism can help protect nature and support local communities.  If you care about

protecting the Earth and want to experience something special, come and explore

Gotjawal Forest.
